cases.text: Open-loop action chunks preserve temporal structure but cannot respond immediately to new contact information. Reactive Diffusion Policy (RDP) retains chunk-level planning while updating individual actions through tactile or force feedback. An asymmetric tokenizer combines an action-only encoder with a contact-conditioned recurrent decoder; a slow diffusion planner predicts latent chunks, and the decoder incorporates fresh contact observations throughout execution. TactAR supplies augmented-reality contact feedback for demonstration collection. Across peeling, wiping, and bimanual lifting, RDP improves task-specific scores over open-loop Diffusion Policy. Under post-contact peeling disturbances, GelSight RDP scores 0.80 versus 0.15 for tactile-input Diffusion Policy, distinguishing reactive architecture from tactile input alone. The slow planner runs at 12 Hz and the decoder at 24 Hz, constrained by GelSight's 25-frame-per-second stream; higher-rate operation remains untested. Trajectories referenced to each chunk's last observation frame and latency-matched execution support smooth transitions.
cases.note: Explained how fresh contact feedback updates actions without replacing chunk-level planning, identified the tactile-input control, and distinguished demonstrated feedback rates from proposed higher-rate operation.

cases.text: With ten trials per variation, GelSight RDP scored 0.90 on peeling and 0.77 on wiping, versus 0.39 and 0.50 for tactile-input Diffusion Policy. Under post-contact peeling disturbances, scores were 0.80 versus 0.15. Across cup types, mixed-sensor RDP scored 0.48 on lifting versus 0.08 for tactile-input Diffusion Policy. These are task-specific scores, not uniform success rates. For post-contact wiping disturbances, shortening baseline chunks from eight to two reduced grasp success from 100% to 20% and task scores from 0.15 to 0.10. Neither tested temporal-ensemble setting matched eight-step GelSight RDP's combination of 100% grasp success and a 0.50 task score.
cases.note: Kept task scores distinct from success rates and specified disturbance conditions. Added the shorter-chunk score change and temporal-ensemble comparison to explain why neither tested alternative recovered RDP's grasping and reactive performance.

cases.text: Joint training on real and simulated demonstrations can improve manipulation policies without exact scene replication. This study co-trains Diffusion Policy with task-aware digital cousins, prior simulation data, or both. Digital cousins preserve the robot, action space, task goal, success criteria, and object and fixture categories, while allowing different object instances and physical and visual properties. Across six real-world tasks on Panda and GR-1 robots, reported average success rises from 45.3% with real-only training to 81.1% with digital cousins, 76.8% with prior simulation, and 83.2% with both. Generated demonstrations broaden training coverage, and evaluations also test unseen objects and positions. Transfer depends on simulation sampling probability and approximate camera alignment, without requiring identical camera models. Prior Panda trajectories are re-rendered to approximately align camera poses, qualifying the use of prior simulation data.
cases.note: Specified digital-cousin invariants and permissible mismatches, separated the aggregate gains from each simulation source, and qualified prior-data reuse by noting camera re-rendering.

cases.text: Reported average success was 45.3% with real-only training, 81.1% with digital cousins, 76.8% with prior simulation, and 83.2% with both. Digital-cousin co-training increased unseen-object success from 33% to 50% on CounterToSinkPnP and from 10% to 80% on CupPnP. With fixed datasets of 20 real and 1,000 simulation demonstrations, CupPnP success fell from 95% at 99% simulation sampling to 60% at 99.9%; increasing sampling probability did not always help. Replacing approximately aligned cameras with default unaligned views reduced success from 67% to 56% on CounterToSinkPnP and from 95% to 70% on CupPnP. Approximate alignment was useful despite unmodeled fisheye distortion in the real humanoid camera.
cases.note: Distinguished sampling probability from fixed dataset size and made its nonmonotonic effect explicit. Added both camera controls and the remaining fisheye mismatch to delimit the alignment claim.

cases.text: CordViP addresses incomplete RGB-D point clouds in dexterous manipulation by constructing model-based hand-object geometry. It samples an object digital twin generated from an image and transforms the samples using FoundationPose's estimated object pose; robot geometry and measured joint configurations provide the hand point cloud. This representation supplies geometry beyond visible depth points under partial occlusion, but requires an adequate object model and continued pose tracking. Separate encoders and cross-attention learn geometrically synthesized contact maps and hand-arm coordination from play data before diffusion-policy training, during which the observation encoder is fine-tuned. With 50 expert demonstrations per task in addition to pretraining, CordViP achieves a reported 90% average success across four base tasks, versus 74% for pose-informed G3Flow. Retaining the representation but removing both pretraining objectives reduces success to 79%, supporting a benefit beyond cleaner geometry alone. Complete hand occlusion can cause tracking failure, and deformable objects challenge the rigid-pose representation.
cases.note: Clarified model-based geometry and continued tracking requirements, identified geometric rather than tactile contact supervision, and separated pose-informed comparisons from fixed-representation ablations. Preserved the complete-occlusion limitation.

cases.text: With 50 demonstrations per task plus separate pretraining, CordViP achieved 85%, 90%, 90%, and 95% success on PickPlace, FlipCup, Assembly, and ArtiManip, respectively, over 20 trials per task. Its reported base-task average was 90%, versus 74% for pose-informed G3Flow and 23% for RGB-D-derived-point-cloud DP3. With CordViP's representation retained, removing both contact and coordination pretraining reduced average success to 79%; removing contact alone yielded 84%, and removing coordination alone yielded 83%. These ablations isolate the contribution of the pretraining objectives from the observation representation. Viewpoint tests used recalibrated cameras, so they do not establish calibration-free transfer. Complete hand occlusion can still disrupt pose tracking; reliable operation with an entirely hidden object remains unsupported.
cases.note: Identified G3Flow as pose-informed and clarified that the pretraining ablations retain the observation representation. Distinguished recalibrated viewpoint transfer from calibration-free operation and partial-occlusion robustness from complete-occlusion reliability.
